analytic.title: Timing Modeling and Analysis for AUTOSAR Schedule Tables

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Schedule table mechanism is an important character of AUTOSAR in addressing its real-time property and flexibility by providing an encapsulation of a static configuration with one or more actions, i.e., events set or tasks activation. As a realtime system, it is non-trivial to analyze schedulability of tasks in AUTOSAR. But it is intractable to analyze schedulability when many schedule tables run at the same time. Moreover, due to the complexity of behavior of schedule tables, the existing schedulability analysis is difficult to be applied to this mechanism. In this paper, we propose a model for AUTOSAR schedule table and give an effective algorithm to assist developers in analyzing schedule tables. A schedule table is formally modeled by a transition system. On the basis of the transition systems, we propose an algorithm to analyze schedulability by checking all the possible schedule scenarios. We show that the problem is polynomial.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Formal methods have been widely and successfully applied to functional properties verification. But unfortunately, it is difficult to verify some non-functional characteristics, which are the key to maintain validity in highly safety-critical realtime systems. Formal analysis on schedulability of tasks is researched. Liu et. al [1] first build a task model for periodic tasks with a period and execution time, then they discuss two scheduling algorithms over the model. Stigge et al. [2] describe a Digraph Real-Time (DRT) model to represent a task and study the feasibility problem on preemptive periodic tasks in a uniprocessor. For analyzing the temporal validity of real-time data objects, Wang et al. [3] give transaction model for tasks with three parameters, a fixed priority, worst-case execution time (WCET) and a relative deadline. The temporal validity of real-time data object is analyzed by periodic update transactions. S. Baruah [4] analyzes schedulability in a general 3-parameter sporadic task model [5] for mixed-criticality concurrent real-time tasks. Moreover, S.Baruah et al. [6] propose a scheduling model for periodic preemptive tasks inspired by control theory. C.Deutschbein et al. [7] present the problem of constructing cyclic executions upon multiprocessors.

AUTOSAR (AUTomotive Open System ARchitecture) [8] is an open and standardized layered software architecture and interfaces. The integration of software modules from different vendors forms the complete architecture. Researchers working on AUTOSAR are rich in progressive and proactive. There have been many studies on analyzing AUTOSAR specification [9]. Peng et al. adopt timed CSP method to model OS and the engine management system (EMS), some safety properties based on CSP models are verified through PAT in [10]. Huang et al. [11] apply formal semantics to describing tasks in AUTOSAR with time protection mechanism. The model predicts whether a task would violate its time constraint, and is implemented in Mathematica tool with a case study. Zhu et al. [12] focus on the timing properties of AUTOSAR and propose an automatic verification framework based on rewriting logic to analyze the timing behaviors. Therefore, research on specification, implementation and verification of AUTOSAR is abundant. For schedulability of the AUTOSAR, both Zhao et al. [13] and Hatvani et al. [14] adopt preemptive threshold to improve the schedulability. Tasks are set with a higher priority and reduced execution time by the stack usage. In order to assist developers in assigning the priorities of tasks, Yoon et al. [15] present a real-time task chain model, which helps to obtain a near-optimal priority assignment from the model. They concentrate on the scheduling of tasks, but there has been very little research on schedule table mechanism. Wang et al. propose a method for generating schedule tables containing periodic tasks with dependence in [16] for the multi-core architectures. However the method does not give the correctness proof of generating schedule tables. Hladik et al. [17]present a mathematical model for schedule tables on top of which them build a number of timing analysis algorithms. Their work models OS interrupt services that can affect the schedulability of a given task, and has great developmental significance to our model. But their models only focus on the case where priorities are all different instead of tasks can shared priorities.

Among those aforementioned researchers, most of them analyze schedulability by modeling tasks, few attentions were given to schedule table mechanism [8], which is an important mechanism in AUTOSAR. A schedule table predefines a pattern of tasks activation by encapsulating a statically defined set of expiry points. The schedulability of schedule tables only depends on the experience of developers and is intractable to be analyzed manually. In order to address the schedulability of schedule tables, it requires a more specific model.

In this paper, we take into consideration the AUTOSAR scheduling with preemptive tasks and schedule tables in a uniprocessor. We provide a formal model for abstracting behaviors of schedule tables and an algorithm to analyze schedulability by verifying all schedule scenarios. In addition, we analyze the complexity of our algorithm as polynomial.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces AUTOSAR schedule tables and schedulability analysis. Section 3 describes formal models of schedule tables. Section 4 presents some definitions and notations. In Section 5, we propose a method by integrating concepts in section 4. Then, experimental results and analysis is given in Section 6. Finally, in Section 7, we conclude our work and describe future work.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND
div.p: In this section, the AUTOSAR schedule table mechanism and its scheduling algorithm are described. We also discuss schedulability problem for AUTOSAR schedule table.

div.head: A. Tasks, Alarms and Scheduling of AUTOSAR
div.p: AUTOSAR considers a task as the minimum unit to be scheduled. A simple application consists of a set of tasks. A task provides the framework for the execution of functions [18]. AUTOSAR provides two types of tasks: extended and basic tasks. Both types are components of complex control software and consist of code blocks. The main difference is that AUTOSAR can receive and record activation request of a basic task which is already activated.

AUTOSAR offers at least one counter. Counters are represented by a counter value, measured in ticks [18]. Based on counters, AUTOSAR drives alarms and schedule tables. Each alarm has a predefined counter value and an action. An alarm will expire when the predefined value is reached. Then, the predefined actions will be executed, which may activate a task or set an event or call an alarm-callback routine. AUTOSAR offers two types of alarms: single and cyclic. Cyclic alarms satisfy the request of processing periodic task.

Each task in AUTOSAR can be assigned to a priority. AUTOSAR uses the static priority and first-come-first-served (FCFS) as its scheduling algorithm. The scheduler always chooses the task with the highest priority to execute. If more than one tasks have the same priority, they are started depending on their order of activation. The priorities are distributed to tasks statically in AUTOSAR. AUTOSAR provides three different scheduling policies: full preemptive, non-preemptive and mixed of preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling. The first means that a task in running state will be transferred into a ready state when a higher priority task gets ready. The second means that once a task starts, it only releases the processor when it terminates.

div.head: B. Schedule Table Mechanism of AUTOSAR
div.p: The schedule table mechanism is a new concept introduced in AUTOSAR. Schedule tables could statically define the pattern of tasks activation by encapsulating a predefined set of expiry points. An expiry point contains one or more actions, which can be either an activation of a task or a setting of an event. Each expiry point has a unique offset in ticks from the start of the schedule table. For a schedule table, the expiry points are processed in order of increasing offset. In addition, Fig. 1: An example repeating schedule table containing three expiry points and three tasks t 1 , t 2 , t 3 .

We give an example in Figure 1 to illustrate the construction of schedule tables. We denote this schedule AUTOSAR offers two types of behavior of schedule tables: single-shot and repeating. On one hand, if a schedule table is configured as single-shot, it will stop at the end. On the other hand, for a repeating schedule table, after the final expiry point has been processed, it loops back to the first expiry point. A repeating schedule table means that tasks are repeated at a period which equals to the schedule table duration.

div.head: C. Schedulability Analysis
div.p: The researches about schedulability analysis focus on the question of whether real-time tasks could satisfy its time property.

In order to figure out the schedulability of real-time systems, several theories have been presented. We can categorize those methods by the existing scheduling algorithm. One of the most common algorithms is the earliest deadline first algorithm (EDF). EDF is considered as an optimized algorithm on preemptive uniprocessor to analyze a set of independent tasks characterized by activated time, deadline and worstcase execution time. For such a dynamic priority scheduling algorithm, the schedulability analysis is co-NP in the strong sense [19].

Since our work focuses on the single processor platform with static priority scheduling, we pay attention to the schedulability analysis based on the response time analysis (RTA) . This approach was proposed by Joseph et al. [20] and improved by Audsley [21]. RTA is appropriate for fixed priority tasks system. This method calculates the worst-case response time, then verify whether the worst-case response time of a task is smaller than its deadline.

div.head: III. MODELING OF SCHEDULE TABLES
div.p: To begin building the model of schedule tables, we need a deterministic specification of AUTOSAR. In particular, AUTOSAR provides multiple features to satisfy the various requirements. For instance, some implemented AUTOSAR allow multiple tasks to share the same priority, while others limit one priority can only map to one task. We only focus on a subset of those features:
• tasks are allowed to share the same priority level;
• there are no extended tasks and events;
• the scheduler is full preemptive;

• scheduling algorithm is static priority and first come first served. For convenience, if a task is assigned to more than one expiry point, we regard them as different tasks. In addition, we assume all schedule tables are repeating. In fact, a repeating schedule table can be transferred to single-shot by changing the final delay into infinitely great. In the remaining part of this section, we propose a formal model for schedule tables, and an example is given.

div.head: IV. DEFINITION AND NOTATION
div.p: In this section, we will give an overview of our algorithm for analyzing schedulability on DSTs basis and introduce some concepts about schedulability problem. Firstly, the schedulability is defined.

div.head: Definition 1. schedulability: A task is schedulable if and only if this task can finish before its deadline in any scenario under static priority and FCFS scheduling algorithm. A set of DSTs is schedulable if and only if all tasks in those DSTs are schedulable.
div.p: Our algorithm follows the Rate Monotonic Analysis (RMA) [22] approach which fits well with our models. The principle of RMA is to check whether the deadline of a task is big enough to accommodate the execution time of itself and all tasks that can interfere it. If tasks in a system all have a sufficiently large deadline then the system is schedulable.

The analysis of our algorithm can be divided into two major phases. The first one is calculating the interference a task can experience within a time interval. In the second step, we determine the boundary of the time interval.

Intuitively, the maximum interference a task can experience is the maximum interference its jobs can experiences. Then the analysis of schedulability of a task can be transformed into check of whether all jobs of this task have a WCRT smaller than deadline. We propose an algorithm to calculate the upper bound on the interference a job can experience.

div.head: A. Computational Requirement Function
div.p: We now focus on the calculation of the interference caused by an instance of expiry point. Due to the static priority and FCFS scheduling algorithm, a job cannot be interrupted by a lower priority job or a job with the same priority but activated later. On this basis, the computational requirement function of expiry points is defined to calculate the interference a job experiences from an instance of expiry point.

div.head: C. Busy Windows
div.p: As we mentioned before, in the first step, we use request functions to calculate the interference a task can experience within a time interval. In the next step, we will determine the boundary of time interval.

Obviously, the upper bound on length of paths in prefix request function θ is less than the deadline of jobs. But the question is how to determine the boundary of θ in suffix request function. Then we introduce the well-known concept: busy windows [24].
Busy window for priority level l is a time interval where the processor continuously processes jobs with priority l or higher priorities.

We explain the concept of busy windows further by an example in Figure 6. The processor continuously processes jobs having a priority higher than or equal to 4 in [0, 21], so the time interval [0, 21] is a busy window for 4.

The characteristic of busy windows implies that jobs that are activated in a busy window always can finish in this busy window. In another word, a job (e * , d * , l * , r * ) in a busy window for l * cannot affect other jobs activated outside the busy window.

If we could find the length of maximum busy window for l, then we can determine the boundary of θ in suffix request function. We use σ l to represent the maximum busy window for l. In order to calculate the maximum of busy windows, we need to define the concept of maximum request function first. div.head: V. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS METHOD
div.p: In the previous section, we give an overview of our algorithm for analyzing tasks' schedulability. In this section, We will propose an integrated method to analyze schedulability of a set of DSTs.

div.head: A. Steps of Method
div.p: For a set of DSTs Γ = {dst 1 , dst 2 , . . . dst n }, the process to analyze schedulability of Γ is divided into four steps:
1) Making a task set τ :
div.formula: τ = {t k |t k ∈ ep j ∧ ep j ∈ dst i ∧ dst i ∈ Γ}.
div.p: Then moving to step(2). 2) If τ is empty, declaring Γ is schedulable. Otherwise, choosing a task with the lowest priority in τ and denoting it as t k = (e, d, l). Then moving to step(3). 3) Using the equation 10 to check whether the task t k is schedulable and moving to step(4).
4) If t k is schedulable, then let τ = τt k and moving to step(2). Otherwise, declaring this set of DSTs is nonschedulable.

div.head: B. Integrated Method
div.p: Two primary algorithms are employed to implement the method as below. There are two global variables: 1) Γ represents the set of DSTs, 2) τ represents the set of all tasks in Γ. return not-pass 5: end if Algorithm 2 aims to verify whether task t k = (e, d, l) can always meet its deadline. If the algorithm finds at least one scenario makes t k to miss it deadline, then returns false.

div.head: C. Discussion about the complexity
div.p: The computational complexity of our algorithm mainly comes from the execution of maximum request functions. We show our algorithm is a polynomial time operation.

The complexity of prefix request functions comes from the maximal length θ of paths which determines the number of tasks need to be considered. Assume there are a total of k tasks in dst i , then the amount of tasks need to be considered in prefix request functions is not more than θ δ(dsti) * k. Because the duration δ(dst i ) and the amount of tasks is fixed, so the prefix request functions prf epj l * ,r * (θ) can be done in O(θ). In a similar way, we can get the complexity of suffix request functions as O(θ).

In Definition 6, maximum request functions compare all of prefix request functions in a dst and find out the maximum value. So the complexity to compute maximum request functions is O(M • θ), where M is the maximum amount of expiry points in a dst.

In Algorithm 2, the source of complexity is the computation of maximum request functions. The times to execute maximum request functions is the product of length of maximum busy windows, amount of DSTs and laxity [25] of tasks. So the complexity of Algorithm 2 is polynomial.
Algorithm 1 calls Algorithm 2 at most |τ | times, where |τ | is the amount of tasks. Then the complexity of our algorithm is still polynomial.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, schedulability of schedule tables in AU-TOSAR is addressed, A directed graph which is called DST, models a schedule table and abstract the behaviors of schedule tables as formal models. An algorithm is proposed based on DST models. The algorithm analyzes the schedulability of schedule tables by covering all the possible schedule scenarios. We also implement a tool about our algorithm to check the effectiveness of the method.

This work has gotten a promising result in analyzing schedule tables on a uniprocessor. Since AUTOSAR specification has introduced multicore operating systems, analyzing schedulability of schedule tables on multiprocessor is important. Basic tasks are taken into consideration in the paper, there are two types of tasks: basic and extended task. Schedulability analysis for extended tasks, which are allowed to synchronize through setting and waiting events, is another interesting topic we would like to pursue. This is only research project, but we believe that the method could perform well in practical implementation.

Table model dst 1 corresponding to schedule table st 1 , where we assume execution time, deadline and priority level of t 1 is 2, 4 and 2 respectively, i.e, t 1 = (2, 4, 2). Similarly, we assume that t 2 = (2, 3, 1) and t 3 = (2, 9, 6).

Algorithm 1 aims to find a non-schedulable task, or proves the set of DSTs is schedulable. The line 1 and 2 check whether the algorithm should terminate. Line 4 implements the step (2) which chooses a task with the lowest priority. The algorithm T ASK AN ALY SIS checks whether the task t k is schedulable. If T ASK AN ALY SIS returns true, then the task is schedulable and will be removed from τ . If the return of T ASK AN ALY SIS is false, then Γ is non-schedulable. The detail of T ASK AN ALY SIS is shown in Algorithm 2.
